While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-of-context versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: Finding Shared Decodable Concepts and their Negations in the Brain
papers.research_question: How can we identify shared decodable concepts (SDCs) in the brain from fMRI data during natural image viewing? The paper proposes a method using contrastive learning and a novel clustering approach to find voxel clusters across participants that represent similar semantic concepts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using contrastive learning and a novel cross-participant DBSCAN clustering to identify shared decodable concepts (SDCs) in the brain from fMRI data, revealing both known and new visuo-semantic categories.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method successfully identifies shared decodable concepts in the brain, including both previously reported and novel visuo-semantic categories, and the use of negative images aids in interpreting the semantic properties of each cluster.
papers.key_findings:
Identified SDCs for known visual features (e.g., orientation tuning in early visual cortex) and semantic concepts (faces, places, bodies).
Discovered two distinct food-related clusters: one driven by color and another by shape, with negative images revealing grayscale images for the color-driven cluster.
Found body-related clusters for legs/hands, motion, and groups of people in extrastriate body area (EBA).
Discovered a numerosity cluster in right intraparietal sulcus (IPS) associated with repeated elements.
Identified clusters for visual perspective (close/far) and lighting conditions.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the stimulus images used in the NSD experiment, which may bias the model towards over-represented categories.
The use of CLIP may introduce biases, as some brain signal may not be captured by CLIP embeddings.
fMRI has limited temporal resolution, restricting the ability to capture rapid neural activity.
The clustering approach might merge concepts within regions of CLIP space that have relatively uniform densities, potentially missing interesting SDCs.
The method is not a replacement for traditional hypothesis-driven experiments.
future_direction: Utilize larger and more diverse fMRI datasets.
Incorporate higher temporal resolution imaging techniques such as EEG or ECoG.
Explore alternative stimulus representations beyond CLIP.
papers.abstract: Prior work has offered evidence for functional localization in the brain; different anatomical regions preferentially activate for certain types of visual input. For example, the fusiform face area preferentially activates for visual stimuli that include a face. However, the spectrum of visual semantics is extensive, and only a few semantically-tuned patches of cortex have so far been identified in the human brain. Using a multimodal (natural language and image) neural network architecture (CLIP) we train a highly accurate contrastive model that maps brain responses during naturalistic image viewing to CLIP embeddings. We then use a novel adaptation of the DBSCAN clustering algorithm to cluster the parameters of these participant-specific contrastive models. This reveals what we call Shared Decodable Concepts (SDCs): clusters in CLIP space that are decodable from common sets of voxels across multiple participants. Examining the images most and least associated with each SDC cluster gives us additional insight into the semantic properties of each SDC. We note SDCs for previously reported visual features (e.g. orientation tuning in early visual cortex) as well as visual semantic concepts such as faces, places and bodies. In cases where our method finds multiple clusters for a visuo-semantic concept, the least associated images allow us to dissociate between confounding factors. For example, we discovered two clusters of food images, one driven by color, the other by shape. We also uncover previously unreported areas such as regions of extrastriate body area (EBA) tuned for legs/hands and sensitivity to numerosity in right intraparietal sulcus, and more. Thus, our contrastive-learning methodology better characterizes new and existing visuo-semantic representations in the brain by leveraging multimodal neural network representations and a novel adaptation of clustering algorithms.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: A framework for the emergence and analysis of language in social learning agents
papers.research_question: How are internal representations structured and optimized for communication between agents in social learning, and how does language emerge from such interactions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a teacher-student reinforcement learning framework with a sparse autoencoder to study emergent communication, showing that student feedback shapes the language embedding to prioritize policy information, improving task performance and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides insights into how language emerges from social interactions and how communication constraints shape internal representations, with implications for generalization in cooperative multi-agent systems.
papers.key_findings:
Providing teacher information to the student leads to higher task completion rates and the ability to generalize to unseen tasks.
Optimizing message content with student feedback improves information encoding, altering the latent structure to focus on policy (goal location and initial action) rather than state space (wall position).
The emergent communication exhibits properties of natural language such as compositionality (topographic similarity) and pressure towards entropy minimization.
Feeding back the student's own task information (closing-the-loop) retains some task-relevant information but results in degraded performance and loss of generalization to unknown goals.
Bi-directional communication (with feedback) is critical for transmitting helpful information and enhances the reconstruction capability of the autoencoder.
future_direction: Understanding how social agents reconcile abstractions from their own experience with those acquired through communication.
Achieving a balance between tutoring and learning in multi-task and multi-agent systems to maintain a relevant and generalizable message space.
papers.abstract: Neural systems have evolved not only to solve environmental challenges through internal representations but also, under social constraints, to communicate these to conspecifics. In this work, we aim to understand the structure of these internal representations and how they may be optimized to transmit pertinent information from one individual to another. Thus, we build on previous teacher-student communication protocols to analyze the formation of individual and shared abstractions and their impact on task performance. We use reinforcement learning in grid-world mazes where a teacher network passes a message to a student to improve task performance. This framework allows us to relate environmental variables with individual and shared representations. We compress high-dimensional task information within a low-dimensional representational space to mimic natural language features. In coherence with previous results, we find that providing teacher information to the student leads to a higher task completion rate and an ability to generalize tasks it has not seen before. Further, optimizing message content to maximize student reward improves information encoding, suggesting that an accurate representation in the space of messages requires bi-directional input. These results highlight the role of language as a common representation among agents and its implications on generalization capabilities.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: VISTA: A Panoramic View of Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How to visually explore and interpret neural network representations by mapping them into semantic 2D spaces to uncover patterns and relationships?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces VISTA, a visualization pipeline that uses clustering and text-to-image models to create semantic 2D maps of neural representations, enabling interactive exploration and interpretation.
papers.conclusion: VISTA provides a visual, interactive method for interpreting neural representations that complements automated techniques and offers deeper insights into model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
VISTA confirms automated interpretations from LLM-based methods, validating its basic functionality.
VISTA discovers additional patterns not captured by automated methods, such as secondary triggers for certain latents.
VISTA reveals unexpected associations in latents, highlighting potential limitations in current automated techniques.
papers.limitation: Potential domain skew between datasets or limitations in automated techniques may affect interpretation, as seen in case study 3.
future_direction: Applying VISTA to a broader range of neural representations and integrating it with existing interpretability pipelines.
papers.abstract: We present VISTA (Visualization of Internal States and Their Associations), a novel pipeline for visually exploring and interpreting neural network representations. VISTA addresses the challenge of analyzing vast multidimensional spaces in modern machine learning models by mapping representations into a semantic 2D space. The resulting collages visually reveal patterns and relationships within internal representations. We demonstrate VISTA's utility by applying it to sparse autoencoder latents uncovering new properties and interpretations. We review the VISTA methodology, present findings from our case study ( https://got.drib.net/latents/ ), and discuss implications for neural network interpretability across various domains of machine learning.

papers.title: Representational models: A common framework for understanding encoding, pattern-component, and representational-similarity analysis
papers.research_question: How do encoding analysis, pattern component modeling (PCM), and representational similarity analysis (RSA) relate to each other, and what is their relative power for adjudicating between competing representational models of neural activity?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a common mathematical framework showing that encoding analysis, pattern component modeling (PCM), and representational similarity analysis (RSA) all evaluate the second moment of the distribution of neural activity profiles, which determines representational geometry and feature decodability.
papers.conclusion: Encoding analysis, PCM, and RSA are closely related methods that test hypotheses about the distribution of neural activity profiles and should be considered complementary components of a unified analytical framework for understanding neural representations.
papers.key_findings:
Pattern component modeling (PCM) implements a likelihood-ratio test and provides the most powerful test between representational models if its assumptions hold.
Encoding analysis, when appropriately regularized (effectively imposing a prior on activity profiles), can perform similarly to PCM.
Representational similarity analysis (RSA) can achieve near-optimal inference power when the unequal variances and statistical dependencies of dissimilarity estimates are properly accounted for.
The three methods are complementary: PCM is analytically tractable and powerful, RSA provides intuitive summary statistics, and encoding analysis enables voxel-wise mapping of features.
All three methods are properly construed as components of a single toolkit for testing hypotheses about neural representations.
papers.limitation:
The methods focus on the second moment of the activity profile distribution; higher-order moments, which may be important for distinguishing between population codes with the same decodability, are not considered.
The framework is based on observational data and does not test causal effects of activity patterns on downstream neural or behavioral responses.
future_direction: Investigating the presence and computational function of non-Gaussian distributions of activity profiles in fMRI or single-cell data.
Extending the framework to include free parameters that change the model structure and to incorporate more detailed measurement models for indirect brain activity measures.
papers.abstract: Representational models specify how activity patterns in populations of neurons (or, more generally, in multivariate brain-activity measurements) relate to sensory stimuli, motor responses, or cognitive processes. In an experimental context, representational models can be defined as hypotheses about the distribution of activity profiles across experimental conditions. Currently, three different methods are being used to test such hypotheses: encoding analysis, pattern component modeling (PCM), and representational similarity analysis (RSA). Here we develop a common mathematical framework for understanding the relationship of these three methods, which share one core commonality: all three evaluate the second moment of the distribution of activity profiles, which determines the representational geometry, and thus how well any feature can be decoded from population activity. Using simulated data for three different experimental designs, we compare the power of the methods to adjudicate between competing representational models. PCM implements a likelihood-ratio test and therefore provides the most powerful test if its assumptions hold. However, the other two approaches-when conducted appropriately-can perform similarly. In encoding analysis, the linear model needs to be appropriately regularized, which effectively imposes a prior on the activity profiles. With such a prior, an encoding model specifies a well-defined distribution of activity profiles. In RSA, the unequal variances and statistical dependencies of the dissimilarity estimates need to be taken into account to reach near-optimal power in inference. The three methods render different aspects of the information explicit (e.g. single-response tuning in encoding analysis and population-response representational dissimilarity in RSA) and have specific advantages in terms of computational demands, ease of use, and extensibility. The three methods are properly construed as complementary components of a single data-analytical toolkit for understanding neural representations on the basis of multivariate brain-activity data.

papers.title: Probing for semantic evidence of composition by means of simple classification tasks
papers.research_question: How can we assess whether sentence-level vector representations capture specific semantic information through composition?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a diagnostic method using targeted classification tasks to probe for specific semantic information in sentence representations, aiming to evaluate composition effectiveness.
papers.conclusion: The diagnostic method provides a targeted way to assess semantic information in sentence representations, with potential for broader application and improvement in dataset construction.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve 100% accuracy on lexical presence tasks (e.g., detecting the word 'school').
On semantic role tasks, Skip-Thought embeddings perform well (91.15% accuracy) while averaging-based models (GloVe, Paragram) perform at chance level, indicating the importance of order information.
The method allows for targeted assessment of semantic information like semantic roles and negation scope in composed sentence representations.
papers.limitation:
Automated sentence generation cannot control for plausibility of generated sentences.
Learning low-dimensional vector representations requires a trade-off between coverage and accessibility of encoded information.
future_direction: Developing a broad-coverage suite of classification tasks for comprehensive assessment of semantic information.
Improving dataset construction with more syntactic variation and plausibility annotation.
papers.abstract: We propose a diagnostic method for probing specific information captured in vector representations of sentence meaning, via simple classification tasks with strategically constructed sentence sets. We identify some key types of semantic information that we might expect to be captured in sentence composition, and illustrate example classification tasks for targeting this information.

papers.title: Prompt-Guided Internal States for Hallucination Detection of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we enhance the cross-domain performance of supervised detectors with only in-domain data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PRISM, a framework that uses prompt-guided internal states to enhance the cross-domain generalization of hallucination detectors by making truthfulness structure more salient and consistent.
papers.conclusion: Suitable prompts enhance the salience and consistency of truthfulness structure in LLMs' internal states, and PRISM improves the generalization performance of hallucination detectors.
papers.key_findings:
Introduction of prompts makes the structure related to text truthfulness more salient in LLMs' internal states.
Prompts increase the consistency of truthfulness structure across different domains.
PRISM significantly improves the generalization performance of existing hallucination detection methods.
Variance ratio can effectively guide prompt selection for better performance.
The framework is effective even in real-world scenarios like the TruthfulQA dataset.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on internal states which may be challenging to access, requiring proxy models.
Does not leverage other information like probability information and generated text.
future_direction: Exploring fully utilizing various types of information produced by LLMs during text generation for more effective hallucination detection.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a variety of tasks in different domains. However, they sometimes generate responses that are logically coherent but factually incorrect or misleading, which is known as LLM hallucinations. Data-driven supervised methods train hallucination detectors by leveraging the internal states of LLMs, but detectors trained on specific domains often struggle to generalize well to other domains. In this paper, we aim to enhance the cross-domain performance of supervised detectors with only in-domain data. We propose a novel framework, prompt-guided internal states for hallucination detection of LLMs, namely PRISM. By utilizing appropriate prompts to guide changes to the structure related to text truthfulness in LLMs' internal states, we make this structure more salient and consistent across texts from different domains. We integrated our framework with existing hallucination detection methods and conducted experiments on datasets from different domains. The experimental results indicate that our framework significantly enhances the cross-domain generalization of existing hallucination detection methods.

papers.title: Self-Sustained Thought Processes in a Dense Associative Network
papers.research_question: How can thought processes be generated autonomously in a dense associative network with overlapping memory states and local reservoirs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a dense associative network (dHAN) with overlapping memory states and local reservoirs that autonomously generates self-sustained thought processes, where memory states serve both as stored information and associative links.
papers.conclusion: Proposes the duality principle for memory states in associative networks and demonstrates that a dense associative network with local reservoirs can autonomously generate thought processes, providing a basis for further research on cognitive tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The model generates autonomous thought processes as time-series of memory states, each associatively connected to its predecessor.
The system can recognize external patterns in a noisy background.
It can focus attention autonomously.
It can represent hierarchical memory states with internal structure.
The dynamics are robust and scalable to large networks.
papers.limitation:
The model may not accurately describe actual thought processes in biological systems.
Further research is needed to demonstrate performance on specific cognitive tasks.
future_direction: Further research to show that the self-regulating system can carry out specific cognitive tasks.
papers.abstract: Several guiding principles for thought processes are proposed and a neural-network-type model implementing these principles is presented and studied. We suggest to consider thinking within an associative network built-up of overlapping memory states. We consider a homogeneous associative network as biological considerations rule out distinct conjunction units between the information (the memories) stored in the brain. We therefore propose that memory states have a dual functionality: They represent on one side the stored information and serve, on the other side, as the associative links in between the different dynamical states of the network which consists of transient attractors. We implement these principles within a generalized winners-take-all neural network with sparse coding and an additional coupling to local reservoirs. We show that this network is capable to generate autonomously a self-sustained time-series of memory states which we identify with a thought process. Each memory state is associatively connected with its predecessor. This system shows several emerging features, it is able (a) to recognize external patterns in a noisy background, (b) to focus attention autonomously and (c) to represent hierarchical memory states with an internal structure.

papers.title: Low-Dimensional Structure in the Space of Language Representations is Reflected in Brain Responses
papers.research_question: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks? Does the low-dimensional structure of these representations correspond to brain responses during language processing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a low-dimensional structure in the space of language representations and shows that this structure can predict how well each representation maps to human brain responses to natural language, suggesting it captures part of the brain's natural language representation hierarchy.
papers.conclusion: The low-dimensional structure in language representations reflects the brain's natural language processing hierarchy, suggesting that the embedding captures some part of the brain's representation structure.
papers.key_findings:
A low-dimensional structure exists in the space of language representations, with the first MDS dimension capturing a progression from word embeddings to syntactic/semantic tasks to next-word embeddings.
The representation embeddings can predict fMRI encoding model performance, indicating a link between the representation space and brain responses.
Projecting the first MDS dimension onto the brain recovers known language processing hierarchies, with early auditory cortex explained by lower-level features and higher-order areas by later layers.
Most pairs of representations can be correctly matched to their brain response patterns using the representation embeddings.
The low-dimensional structure is consistent across different language models and translation models.
papers.limitation: Negative discriminability scores for some representation pairs, possibly due to disconnect between task affinities and brain representations, e.g., for GloVe next-word embedding.
papers.abstract: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks? We answer this question by adapting an encoder-decoder transfer learning method from computer vision to investigate the structure among 100 different feature spaces extracted from hidden representations of various networks trained on language tasks. This method reveals a low-dimensional structure where language models and translation models smoothly interpolate between word embeddings, syntactic and semantic tasks, and future word embeddings. We call this low-dimensional structure a language representation embedding because it encodes the relationships between representations needed to process language for a variety of NLP tasks. We find that this representation embedding can predict how well each individual feature space maps to human brain responses to natural language stimuli recorded using fMRI. Additionally, we find that the principal dimension of this structure can be used to create a metric which highlights the brain's natural language processing hierarchy. This suggests that the embedding captures some part of the brain's natural language representation structure.

papers.title: Towards Utilising a Range of Neural Activations for Comprehending Representational Associations
papers.research_question: What is the value of studying non-maximal neuron activations for understanding model representations and mitigating spurious correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that non-maximal activations contain valuable information about model representations and introduces MID, a method to curate data from mid-range logits to mitigate spurious correlations.
papers.conclusion: Examining non-maximal activations is practical for locating entangled concepts and understanding representations, and MID effectively improves model robustness to spurious correlations.
papers.key_findings:
Mid-level activations reveal spurious patterns not visible in maximal activations.
Mid-level activations help identify mislabeled samples.
MID improves worst-group accuracy on benchmark datasets.
Non-maximal activations provide insights into concept entanglement in model representations.
MID beats state-of-the-art methods that require no group labels for mitigating spurious correlations.
papers.limitation: The framework involves human intervention for cluster interpretation, which may not be fully automated.
future_direction: Extending to latent layers and generative models
Investigating concept disentanglement in concept bottleneck models
Automating cluster interpretation
papers.abstract: Recent efforts to understand intermediate representations in deep neural networks have commonly attempted to label individual neurons and combinations of neurons that make up linear directions in the latent space by examining extremal neuron activations and the highest direction projections. In this paper, we show that this approach, although yielding a good approximation for many purposes, fails to capture valuable information about the behaviour of a representation. Neural network activations are generally dense, and so a more complex, but realistic scenario is that linear directions encode information at various levels of stimulation. We hypothesise that non-extremal level activations contain complex information worth investigating, such as statistical associations, and thus may be used to locate confounding human interpretable concepts. We explore the value of studying a range of neuron activations by taking the case of mid-level output neuron activations and demonstrate on a synthetic dataset how they can inform us about aspects of representations in the penultimate layer not evident through analysing maximal activations alone. We use our findings to develop a method to curate data from mid-range logit samples for retraining to mitigate spurious correlations, or confounding concepts in the penultimate layer, on real benchmark datasets. The success of our method exemplifies the utility of inspecting non-maximal activations to extract complex relationships learned by models.

papers.title: SCIURus: Shared Circuits for Interpretable Uncertainty Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do the factuality of generated responses and a model's uncertainty originate in separate or shared circuits within the model architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a language model's uncertainty and the factuality of its generated answers are produced by shared circuits in the model, rather than separate ones.
papers.conclusion: The results broadly support the shared circuits hypothesis, suggesting that P(IK) probing elicits introspective, interpretable uncertainty estimates and that uncertainty quantification in LLMs may largely rely on the same circuitry used for question-answering.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing experiments show that the same model components (layers, attention heads) affect both the model's correct-token probability and the P(IK) probe's confidence estimate.
Zero-ablation experiments (both leave-one-out and COAR) across multiple models and datasets support the shared circuits hypothesis, with changes in model accuracy and probe output being highly correlated.
The P(IK) probe's uncertainty representation often remains calibrated even after interventions that damage model performance.
The shared circuits hypothesis holds across a range of models (Llama 2/3, Gemma 2) and datasets (TriviaQA, WebQuestions, MMLU, ARC, CounterFact).
Some discrepancies occur, such as when answer tokens appear in the question, where restorations can suppress model accuracy but not probe confidence.
papers.limitation:
Zero-ablation may lack specificity because zeroing out a component can severely damage general language coherence, not just task-specific information flow.
Causal tracing may miss important circuits when information flows along multiple parallel paths, as restoring a single path may not show a substantial effect.
future_direction: Analyze the mechanisms responsible for P(IK) estimates in greater detail.
Apply P(IK) probing as an interpretability tool to study phenomena like hallucination in LLMs.
Perform similar analyses on other uncertainty quantification methods, such as verbalized uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Carter Teplica, Yixin Liu, Arman Cohan, Tim G. J. Rudner. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Building artificial neural circuits for domain-general cognition: a primer on brain-inspired systems-level architecture
papers.research_question: How can principles from the brain's systems-level architecture, specifically recurrence, communicability, and short-term topological changes, inform the design of artificial neural networks for domain-general cognition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reviews three brain-inspired architectural principles (global recurrence, communicability, and short-term topological changes) that could serve as inductive biases for building artificial neural networks capable of domain-general cognition.
papers.conclusion: A systems-level view of the brain, focusing on recurrence, communication, and rapid structural changes, can provide valuable guidance for building artificial intelligence that achieves domain-general problem-solving, and testing these principles in artificial systems may help understand biological cognition.
papers.key_findings:
The brain's Multiple Demand system uses global recurrence to integrate and broadcast information across distributed regions, a feature that may be necessary for domain-general cognition in artificial systems.
Optimizing communicability in large-scale networks can improve information flow between modules, which is crucial for complex multimodal systems.
Short-term topological changes (e.g., via local learning rules) enable flexible reconfiguration of neural circuits, supporting rapid adaptation and abstract problem-solving.
Current artificial neural networks lack these system-level properties, and incorporating them could enhance their flexibility and generalization.
future_direction: Incorporating global recurrent loops into artificial neural networks to enable widespread integration and broadcasting of abstract knowledge.
Optimizing communicability in large-scale modular networks to improve information flow between components.
Enabling short-term topological changes through local learning rules to allow rapid reconfiguration and flexible problem-solving.
papers.abstract: There is a concerted effort to build domain-general artificial intelligence in the form of universal neural network models with sufficient computational flexibility to solve a wide variety of cognitive tasks but without requiring fine-tuning on individual problem spaces and domains. To do this, models need appropriate priors and inductive biases, such that trained models can generalise to out-of-distribution examples and new problem sets. Here we provide an overview of the hallmarks endowing biological neural networks with the functionality needed for flexible cognition, in order to establish which features might also be important to achieve similar functionality in artificial systems. We specifically discuss the role of system-level distribution of network communication and recurrence, in addition to the role of short-term topological changes for efficient local computation. As machine learning models become more complex, these principles may provide valuable directions in an otherwise vast space of possible architectures. In addition, testing these inductive biases within artificial systems may help us to understand the biological principles underlying domain-general cognition.

papers.title: Predictive Concept Decoders: Training Scalable End-to-End Interpretability Assistants
papers.research_question: How can we train interpretability assistants to accurately predict model behavior from internal activations through an end-to-end training objective with a communication bottleneck?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Predictive Concept Decoders (PCDs), an end-to-end trainable architecture for interpretability that compresses model activations into sparse concepts and uses a decoder to answer questions about model behavior, showing favorable scaling properties.
papers.conclusion: Predictive Concept Decoders offer a scalable approach to interpretability that can surface latent information in model activations, with applications in detecting atypical behaviors and auditing model reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
PCDs can detect jailbreaks, secret hints, and implanted latent concepts, and accurately surface latent user attributes.
PCDs reveal information that models fail to self-report, such as hint usage and jailbreak awareness that prompting cannot elicit.
The auto-interp score of the bottleneck concepts improves with pretraining data, and at high sparsity outperforms SAE features trained on the same data.
Decoder performance improves with scale and outperforms both direct prompting and LatentQA, a baseline without the sparse bottleneck.
The encoder's sparse concepts provide auditable explanations, allowing predictions to be traced to a small set of inspectable concepts.
papers.limitation:
KL-based objectives (used in PCDs and KL SAEs) may saturate earlier than L2 reconstruction objectives, potentially because the KL objective is too 'easy' to optimize, leading to a sparser signal.
Without an auxiliary loss, many encoder concepts become inactive ('dead') during training, degrading the quality of the learned dictionary.
future_direction: Addressing the plateau in encoder interpretability metrics observed with KL-based objectives.
papers.abstract: Interpreting the internal activations of neural networks can produce more faithful explanations of their behavior, but is difficult due to the complex structure of activation space. Existing approaches to scalable interpretability use hand-designed agents that make and test hypotheses about how internal activations relate to external behavior. We propose to instead turn this task into an end-to-end training objective, by training interpretability assistants to accurately predict model behavior from activations through a communication bottleneck. Specifically, an encoder compresses activations to a sparse list of concepts, and a decoder reads this list and answers a natural language question about the model. We show how to pretrain this assistant on large unstructured data, then finetune it to answer questions. The resulting architecture, which we call a Predictive Concept Decoder, enjoys favorable scaling properties: the auto-interp score of the bottleneck concepts improves with data, as does the performance on downstream applications. Specifically, PCDs can detect jailbreaks, secret hints, and implanted latent concepts, and are able to accurately surface latent user attributes.

papers.title: Language Representation Projection: Can We Transfer Factual Knowledge across Languages in Multilingual Language Models?
papers.research_question: Can cross-lingual alignment of representation spaces enable factual knowledge transfer across languages? Specifically, can we transfer factual knowledge from English to non-English languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes LRP2, a parameter-free method that projects representations between languages to align representation spaces, which improves factual knowledge retrieval and transfer across languages in multilingual language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper confirms that cross-lingual alignment of representation spaces enables factual knowledge transfer across languages, and proposes LRP2 as an effective method for this transfer.
papers.key_findings:
LRP2 improves factual knowledge retrieval accuracy and cross-lingual transferability for non-English languages.
LRP2 aligns representation spaces: LIRP projects non-English representations to English-like ones, and LSRP projects them back to the non-English space.
LRP2 increases the overlap of knowledge neurons between English and non-English languages, indicating enhanced cross-lingual knowledge transfer.
Cross-lingual knowledge neurons exist in multilingual pretrained language models.
Different languages require different optimal layer configurations for the LIRP and LSRP modules, indicating varying degrees of representation alignment needed.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of LRP2 heavily relies on the inherent capabilities of multilingual pretrained language models.
Experiments are limited to two relatively small models due to limited compute resources.
future_direction: Investigate LRP2 on larger language models.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pretrained language models serve as repositories of multilingual factual knowledge. Nevertheless, a substantial performance gap of factual knowledge probing exists between high-resource languages and low-resource languages, suggesting limited implicit factual knowledge transfer across languages in multilingual pretrained language models. This paper investigates the feasibility of explicitly transferring relatively rich factual knowledge from English to non-English languages. To accomplish this, we propose two parameter-free Language Representation Projection modules (LRP2). The first module converts non-English representations into English-like equivalents, while the second module reverts English-like representations back into representations of the corresponding non-English language. Experimental results on the mLAMA dataset demonstrate that LRP2 significantly improves factual knowledge retrieval accuracy and facilitates knowledge transferability across diverse non-English languages. We further investigate the working mechanism of LRP2 from the perspectives of representation space and cross-lingual knowledge neuron.

papers.title: Emergence of Concepts in DNNs?
papers.research_question: How do existing methods identify concepts in DNNs, and how are conceptual spaces shaped by the tradeoff between predictive accuracy and compression?
papers.core_contribution: Reviews and critiques methods for identifying concepts in DNNs, highlighting limitations due to reliance on partial extensions and the underexplored role of conceptual spaces shaped by accuracy-compression tradeoffs.
papers.conclusion: While DNNs can represent inferential relations between concepts, current methods for identifying these concepts are limited, and understanding holistic conceptual spaces requires new approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Network dissection, feature visualization, and TCAV methods for identifying concepts in DNNs rely on partial extensions or optimization, leading to philosophical issues like indeterminacy of reference.
DNNs can learn concepts shared by multiple predicted classes, indicating representation of non-trivial inferential relations beyond mere extensions.
Conceptual spaces in DNNs are shaped by a tradeoff between predictive accuracy and compression, as illustrated by the Information Bottleneck framework and color naming examples.
Polysemantic neurons suggest that concepts compete for limited representational space, leading to compressed or mixed representations.
Robustness analysis by combining multiple methods could improve reliability, but absolute confirmation of concepts remains challenging.
papers.limitation:
Methods for identifying concepts rely on partial extensions, which underdetermine meaning and face indeterminacy of reference.
Existing methods are limited to extracting local or linear information, not capturing distributed or non-linear representations.
The identification of conceptual spaces and how they arise from accuracy-compression tradeoffs is underexplored.
future_direction: Combining different methods for robustness analysis to increase reliability in concept identification.
Using synthetic datasets with labeled intermediate concepts to test and improve methods for identifying concepts.
Developing methods to understand how entire conceptual spaces are formed holistically in DNNs.
papers.abstract: The present paper reviews and discusses work from computer science that proposes to identify concepts in internal representations (hidden layers) of DNNs. It is examined, first, how existing methods actually identify concepts that are supposedly represented in DNNs. Second, it is discussed how conceptual spaces -- sets of concepts in internal representations -- are shaped by a tradeoff between predictive accuracy and compression. These issues are critically examined by drawing on philosophy. While there is evidence that DNNs able to represent non-trivial inferential relations between concepts, our ability to identify concepts is severely limited.

papers.title: Toward universal steering and monitoring of AI models
papers.research_question: How can we extract linear representations of concepts from internal activations of AI models to enable steering and monitoring?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a scalable method using Recursive Feature Machines (RFM) to extract linear concept representations from internal model activations, enabling effective steering and monitoring across diverse models and concepts.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the power of using internal representations for steering and monitoring AI models, providing a cost-efficient alternative to fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
The RFM method can extract concept vectors that enable steering and monitoring in LLMs, VLMs, and reasoning models.
Concept vectors are transferable across languages and can be combined for multi-concept steering.
Newer, larger models are more steerable, and steering can improve model capabilities beyond standard prompting.
Concept representations are effective for monitoring misaligned content (hallucinations, toxic content) and outperform judge models.
The method is scalable, requiring under one minute and fewer than 500 training samples on a single GPU.
papers.abstract: Modern AI models contain much of human knowledge, yet understanding of their internal representation of this knowledge remains elusive. Characterizing the structure and properties of this representation will lead to improvements in model capabilities and development of effective safeguards. Building on recent advances in feature learning, we develop an effective, scalable approach for extracting linear representations of general concepts in large-scale AI models (language models, vision-language models, and reasoning models). We show how these representations enable model steering, through which we expose vulnerabilities, mitigate misaligned behaviors, and improve model capabilities. Additionally, we demonstrate that concept representations are remarkably transferable across human languages and combinable to enable multi-concept steering. Through quantitative analysis across hundreds of concepts, we find that newer, larger models are more steerable and steering can improve model capabilities beyond standard prompting. We show how concept representations are effective for monitoring misaligned content (hallucinations, toxic content). We demonstrate that predictive models built using concept representations are more accurate for monitoring misaligned content than using models that judge outputs directly. Together, our results illustrate the power of using internal representations to map the knowledge in AI models, advance AI safety, and improve model capabilities.

papers.title: Integrated deep visual and semantic attractor neural networks predict fMRI pattern-information along the ventral object processing pathway
papers.research_question: How does visual processing activate and interact with semantic representations during object recognition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper combines a deep convolutional neural network model of vision with an attractor network model of semantics and shows that different stages of this integrated model explain fMRI pattern-information along the ventral object processing pathway.
papers.conclusion: The combined visuo-semantic model provides a proof-of-principle for how visual and semantic processing can be integrated and accounts for neural data along the ventral stream, showing a gradient from visual to semantic representations.
papers.key_findings:
Visual layers of the DNN best explain activation patterns in early visual cortex.
Posterior ventral temporal cortex is best explained by early stages of the semantic attractor network, corresponding to initial semantic processing.
Perirhinal cortex is best explained by the final stages of the semantic attractor network, when detailed semantic representations are activated.
The model learns associations between high-level visual regularities and semantic features, with shared semantic features activating more rapidly than distinctive features.
The model implements a general-to-specific account of object processing, where coarse-grained semantics activate before fine-grained details.
papers.limitation:
The model is trained in two separate stages (pre-trained DNN then attractor network), so there is no possibility for semantic representations to influence earlier visual layers via feedback.
The model is trained and tested on a specific set of images and has not been evaluated on its ability to generalize semantic patterns to previously unseen images.
future_direction: Training the visual and semantic components of the model together in an end-to-end manner.
Exploring architectures with direct connections from early visual layers to semantics, semantic-to-visual top-down connections, and lateral recurrent connections within visual layers.
Testing the model's semantic patterns for previously unseen images.
papers.abstract: Recognising an object involves rapid visual processing and activation of semantic knowledge about the object, but how visual processing activates and interacts with semantic representations remains unclear. Cognitive neuroscience research has shown that while visual processing involves posterior regions along the ventral stream, object meaning involves more anterior regions, especially perirhinal cortex. Here we investigate visuo-semantic processing by combining a deep neural network model of vision with an attractor network model of semantics, such that visual information maps onto object meanings represented as activation patterns across features. In the combined model, concept activation is driven by visual input and co-occurrence of semantic features, consistent with neurocognitive accounts. We tested the model's ability to explain fMRI data where participants named objects. Visual layers explained activation patterns in early visual cortex, whereas pattern-information in perirhinal cortex was best explained by later stages of the attractor network, when detailed semantic representations are activated. Posterior ventral temporal cortex was best explained by intermediate stages corresponding to initial semantic processing, when visual information has the greatest influence on the emerging semantic representation. These results provide proof of principle of how a mechanistic model of combined visuo-semantic processing can account for pattern-information in the ventral stream.

papers.title: Quiet Feature Learning in Algorithmic Tasks
papers.research_question: Do Transformer-based models learn meaningful internal representations (quiet features) before showing improvement in task loss, and are these features causally necessary for performance?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer-based models learn 'quiet features' (intermediate algorithmic computations) during a slow phase where task loss is stagnant, and these features are causally necessary for the subsequent sharp drop in loss.
papers.conclusion: Transformer-based models encode important intermediate computations well before they show significant gains in next-token prediction, revealing a gap between internal representation learning and external task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Phase transitions occur during learning: validation loss shows a slow phase with minimal improvement followed by a fast phase of rapid decrease.
Quiet features, representing intermediate algorithmic computations, are learned during the slow phase before any decrease in task loss.
Ablation experiments show that quiet features are causally necessary for task performance.
Feature learning curves can exhibit a U-shape, where probing loss for some quiet features increases after the phase transition, suggesting representation changes.
Phase transitions are observed across different compute budgets, model sizes, dataset sizes, and within individual training runs.
future_direction: Developing theoretical frameworks to explain why models accumulate latent subroutines before observable metric improvements.
Extending the analysis to larger, more complex models and natural-language settings.
Motivating new methods for probing and monitoring internal learning dynamics.
papers.abstract: We train Transformer-based language models on ten foundational algorithmic tasks and observe pronounced phase transitions in their loss curves that deviate from established power-law scaling trends. Over large ranges of compute, the validation loss barely improves, then abruptly decreases. Probing the models' internal representations reveals that quiet features are learned prior to any decrease in task loss. These quiet features represent intermediate algorithmic computations that do not by themselves improve the output loss. Ablation experiments demonstrate that individual quiet features are causally necessary for task performance. Our results demonstrate that substantial representational progress can remain hidden beneath an apparently flat loss curve, challenging the prevailing use of cross-entropy as a proxy for learning and motivating richer diagnostics for monitoring model training.

papers.title: Ablation of a Robot's Brain: Neural Networks Under a Knife
papers.research_question: How can ablation be used to determine the structure of information in neural networks, and what similarities exist between biological and artificial neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an ablation-based method to analyze neural networks, demonstrating that artificial neural networks exhibit robustness to damage and localization of function similar to biological neural networks.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates similarities in organization and information storage between biological and artificial neural networks through ablation, highlighting the need for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Ablation of neuron groups leads to consistent output shifts, showing localization of function.
Networks are robust to damage, with removal of single groups not eliminating task performance.
Clustering identifies 6 distinct functional roles for neuron groups.
Analogous functional regions exist across different training trials.
papers.limitation:
Granularity of ablations is coarse; future studies need finer-scale analysis.
Limited dataset due to reinforcement learning and real-time training constraints.
future_direction: Investigate similarities at different scales of ablation granularity.
Use larger datasets for more comprehensive analysis.
Further research to develop better theoretical understanding.
papers.abstract: It is still not fully understood exactly how neural networks are able to solve the complex tasks that have recently pushed AI research forward. We present a novel method for determining how information is structured inside a neural network. Using ablation (a neuroscience technique for cutting away parts of a brain to determine their function), we approach several neural network architectures from a biological perspective. Through an analysis of this method's results, we examine important similarities between biological and artificial neural networks to search for the implicit knowledge locked away in the network's weights.

papers.title: Identification of untrained class data using neuron clusters
papers.research_question: Does a set of neurons (class neuron cluster) exist for each class that captures class characteristics, and can the similarity between such neuron sets be used to identify data from untrained classes?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a Class Neuron Cluster (CNC) method for identifying untrained class data by analyzing neuron activations, without modifying the model structure, achieving high accuracy with low computational cost.
papers.conclusion: The proposed CNC method effectively identifies untrained class data by analyzing neuron activations, offering a model-independent approach with high accuracy and low computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
The CNC method identifies untrained class data with accuracy over 85% on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and STL-10 datasets.
More data for CNC identification leads to higher accuracy, while more complex datasets lead to lower accuracy.
CNC similarity analysis shows that classes with similar characteristics have higher similarity between their CNCs.
The method does not affect the model's classification performance and has low computational cost.
The method outperforms existing data-based and model-based methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.
papers.limitation:
Performance depends on the number of data used for CNC identification and the activation rate threshold.
Tested only on image datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, STL-10).
future_direction: Extend the method to identify mutated data (e.g., from adversarial attacks) and data generated by GANs.
Apply the method to other types of data beyond images.
Explore the use of CNC in other models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Abstract Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), a representative type of deep neural networks, are used in various fields. There are problems that should be solved to operate CNN in the real-world. In real-world operating environments, the CNN’s performance may be degraded due to data of untrained types, which limits its operability. In this study, we propose a method for identifying data of a type that the model has not trained on based on the neuron cluster, a set of neurons activated based on the type of input data. In experiments performed on the ResNet model with the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and STL-10 datasets, the proposed method identifies data of untrained and trained types with an accuracy of 85% or higher. The more data used for neuron cluster identification, the higher the accuracy; conversely, the more complex the dataset's characteristics, the lower the accuracy. The proposed method uses only the information of activated neurons without any addition or modification of the model’s structure; hence, the computational cost is low without affecting the classification performance of the model.

papers.title: VAST: The Valence-Assessing Semantics Test for Contextualizing Language\n Models
papers.research_question: How can we measure the semantic quality of contextualized word embeddings and understand the effects of contextualization, tokenization, and model-specific geometry on word-level semantics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces V AST, an intrinsic evaluation task for contextualized word embeddings that uses valence to measure word-level semantics and reveals how contextualization, tokenization, and high-magnitude neurons affect semantic representations.
papers.conclusion: V AST is a novel intrinsic evaluation task that allows researchers to measure and isolate word-level semantics in CWEs, revealing how context changes CWE semantics, how tokenization leads to a different encoding process for uncommon words, and how high-magnitude neurons mask word-level semantics and social biases.
papers.key_findings:
V AST shows that context alters CWE semantics in the top layers of GPT-2, with scores diverging between contextual settings after layer 8.
Multiply tokenized words are not semantically encoded until layer 8 in GPT-2, indicating a different encoding process for singly vs. multiply tokenized words.
High-magnitude neurons in the top layer mask word-level semantics, and nullifying non-semantic principal components recovers semantics (Pearson's ρ improves from .32 to .76 in the top layer).
After isolating semantics, V AST improves over prior work on word similarity tasks (e.g., .50 on SimLex-999 vs. previous best .45 for GPT-2).
Isolating semantics reveals more stereotype-congruent biases in 8 of 10 WEA T tests, indicating that non-semantic structures also mask social biases.
papers.limitation:
Sentence structure may affect CWEs in ways that distort semantic analysis beyond what V AST detects.
The effect size for some biases, especially for names, varies with the number of PCs nullified.
V AST does not deal with the senses of polysemous words.
V AST's tokenization experiment does not control for word frequency.
future_direction: Address the effect of sentence structure on CWEs.
Study the variation in bias effect sizes with the number of PCs nullified.
Extend V AST to handle polysemous words.
papers.abstract:
VAST, the Valence-Assessing Semantics Test, is a novel intrinsic evaluation
task for contextualized word embeddings (CWEs). VAST uses valence, the
association of a word with pleasantness, to measure the correspondence of
word-level LM semantics with widely used human judgments, and examines the
effects of contextualization, tokenization, and LM-specific geometry. Because
prior research has found that CWEs from GPT-2 perform poorly on other intrinsic
evaluations, we select GPT-2 as our primary subject, and include results
showing that VAST is useful for 7 other LMs, and can be used in 7 languages.
GPT-2 results show that the semantics of a word incorporate the semantics of
context in layers closer to model output, such that VAST scores diverge between
our contextual settings, ranging from Pearson's rho of .55 to .77 in layer 11.
We also show that multiply tokenized words are not semantically encoded until
layer 8, where they achieve Pearson's rho of .46, indicating the presence of an
encoding process for multiply tokenized words which differs from that of singly
tokenized words, for which rho is highest in layer 0. We find that a few
neurons with values having greater magnitude than the rest mask word-level
semantics in GPT-2's top layer, but that word-level semantics can be recovered
by nullifying non-semantic principal components: Pearson's rho in the top layer
improves from .32 to .76. After isolating semantics, we show the utility of
VAST for understanding LM semantics via improvements over related work on four
word similarity tasks, with a score of .50 on SimLex-999, better than the
previous best of .45 for GPT-2. Finally, we show that 8 of 10 WEAT bias tests,
which compare differences in word embedding associations between groups of
words, exhibit more stereotype-congruent biases after isolating semantics,
indicating that non-semantic structures in LMs also mask biases.

papers.title: Trigger-Argument based Explanation for Event Detection
papers.research_question: How can event structure knowledge (trigger-argument structures) be utilized to generate faithful, neuron-level explanations for Event Detection (ED) models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces TAE, a model-agnostic method that uses trigger-argument event structures to generate faithful and human-understandable neuron-level explanations for Event Detection models.
papers.conclusion: TAE is an effective method for explaining ED models, providing more faithful and human-understandable explanations by leveraging event structure knowledge at the neuron level.
papers.key_findings:
TAE achieves better performance on support (faithfulness) and sparsity metrics compared to baseline explanation methods.
The group mechanism in TAE effectively clusters neurons corresponding to event arguments, improving interpretability.
Trigger-argument features lead to more faithful explanations than word-level features.
TAE provides explanations that not only highlight important text features but also reveal how they contribute to the final prediction via event roles.
papers.limitation:
TAE depends on an automatic parser for event structure information; parser errors can impact performance.
The method is restricted to text-based event explanation and has not been explored in multi-modal settings.
future_direction: Using explanations to further improve ED classification and downstream applications.
Exploring ED and its explanations under the multi-modal setting.
Investigating event relation extraction and high-quality methods for constructing and utilizing Event Knowledge Graphs (EKGs).
papers.abstract: Event Detection (ED) is a critical task that aims to identify events of certain types in plain text. Neural models have achieved great success on ED, thus coming with a desire for higher interpretability. Existing works mainly exploit words or phrases of the input text to explain models' inner mechanisms. However, for ED, the event structure, comprising of an event trigger and a set of arguments, are more enlightening clues to explain model behaviors. To this end, we propose a Trigger-Argument based Explanation method (TAE), which can utilize event structure knowledge to uncover a faithful interpretation for the existing ED models at neuron level. Specifically, we design group, sparsity, support mechanisms to construct the event structure from structuralization, compactness, and faithfulness perspectives. We evaluate our model on the large-scale MAVEN and the widely-used ACE 2005 datasets, and observe that TAE is able to reveal the process by which the model predicts. Experimental results also demonstrate that TAE can not only improve the interpretability on standard evaluation metrics, but also effectively facilitate the human understanding.

papers.title: A Property Induction Framework for Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent can experience from language contribute to conceptual knowledge? Specifically, do neural language models show a taxonomic bias when generalizing novel properties?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for property induction with neural language models and uses it to show that LMs exhibit a taxonomic bias when generalizing novel properties.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LMs exhibit a taxonomic bias when generalizing novel properties, likely reflecting latent taxonomic knowledge acquired during pre-training, which guides inductive generalizations.
papers.key_findings:
LMs fine-tuned for property judgment achieve high F1 scores on unseen properties, indicating they can rely on generalizable property knowledge.
LMs show a preference to generalize novel properties to concepts within the same taxonomic category rather than outside, suggesting a taxonomic bias.
The taxonomic bias persists even when concepts have greater property overlap with concepts from a different category, indicating the bias is not solely due to training data statistics.
Generalization strength increases with the number of adaptation concepts, mirroring human premise monotonicity effects.
Property overlap between adaptation and generalization sets predicts generalization scores, but taxonomic bias remains significant beyond this.
papers.limitation: The source of the taxonomic bias in the models cannot be precisely identified.
future_direction: Testing a broader range of inductive phenomena observed in humans using the framework.
Investigating inductive generalizations guided by intuitive theories (e.g., biological vs. behavioral properties).
Exploring the context-specific flexibility of LM representations and domain knowledge acquisition.
papers.abstract: To what extent can experience from language contribute to our conceptual knowledge? Computational explorations of this question have shed light on the ability of powerful neural language models (LMs) -- informed solely through text input -- to encode and elicit information about concepts and properties. To extend this line of research, we present a framework that uses neural-network language models (LMs) to perform property induction -- a task in which humans generalize novel property knowledge (has sesamoid bones) from one or more concepts (robins) to others (sparrows, canaries). Patterns of property induction observed in humans have shed considerable light on the nature and organization of human conceptual knowledge. Inspired by this insight, we use our framework to explore the property inductions of LMs, and find that they show an inductive preference to generalize novel properties on the basis of category membership, suggesting the presence of a taxonomic bias in their representations.

papers.title: Neuropsychology and Explainability of AI: A Distributional Approach to the Relationship Between Activation Similarity of Neural Categories in Synthetic Cognition
papers.research_question: Is the degree of membership (activation level) of tokens to the category associated with a neuron related to their level of similarity (cosine similarity)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates a process of categorical convergence, where as the activation levels of successive core tokens increase, the categorical variability (cosine similarity) of these tokens decreases.
papers.conclusion: The categorical segment constructed by a neuron can be decomposed into a vector space of categorical sub-dimensions; tokens with high activation involve these sub-dimensions jointly, leading to observed categorical convergence.
papers.key_findings:
The number of low extreme cosine similarity values decreases as activation values increase.
A majority of neurons show a positive relationship between cosine similarity and activation level, though the effect is often small.
The average cosine similarity for pairs of tokens with high activations is systematically higher than for pairs with low activations.
The relationship between activation and cosine similarity is better modeled by an exponential function than a linear one.
Highly activated tokens can be interpreted as prototypes of the synthetic categories constructed by neurons.
future_direction: A 'genetic' study aimed at explaining the categorical abstraction produced by artificial neurons in terms of the reconstruction of the categorical segmentations of their most influential precursor neurons.
papers.abstract: We propose a neuropsychological approach to the explainability of artificial neural networks, which involves using concepts from human cognitive psychology as relevant heuristic references for developing synthetic explanatory frameworks that align with human modes of thought. The analogical concepts mobilized here, which are intended to create such an epistemological bridge, are those of categorization and similarity, as these notions are particularly suited to the categorical "nature" of the reconstructive information processing performed by artificial neural networks. Our study aims to reveal a unique process of synthetic cognition, that of the categorical convergence of highly activated tokens. We attempt to explain this process with the idea that the categorical segment created by a neuron is actually the result of a superposition of categorical sub-dimensions within its input vector space.

papers.title: Activation-Space Personality Steering: Hybrid Layer Selection for Stable Trait Control in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we reliably control or align personality traits (Big Five) in Large Language Model generation through targeted interventions in the model's internal activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a pipeline for personality steering in LLMs that extracts low-rank trait directions from activations and uses a hybrid (verified + dynamic) layer selection strategy to inject these directions into the residual stream, enabling precise control of Big Five trait expression without retraining.
papers.conclusion: The proposed activation-space personality steering framework with hybrid layer selection provides a robust and effective method for controlling personality traits in LLMs, bridging psychological theory and practical model alignment without degrading core capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Personality traits in LLMs occupy a low-rank shared subspace, with top three principal components explaining over 90% of variance.
A hybrid layer selection strategy (combining offline verified layers and prompt-specific dynamic layers) yields stronger and more stable trait steering than using either component alone.
The steering method effectively shifts trait expression in both positive and negative directions while largely preserving the model's fluency and general reasoning capabilities (as measured by MMLU and ARC-Challenge).
The learned trait direction vectors exhibit structured correlations (e.g., between Openness and Extraversion), indicating shared representational structure for personality-related behaviors.
Steering effectiveness varies across model families, with some dependencies observed between traits when steered simultaneously.
papers.limitation:
Steering effectiveness is greater on some model families (e.g., Llama, Mistral) than others (e.g., Qwen).
Dependencies between traits (e.g., agreeableness and openness) can complicate independent steering, and applying orthogonality to remove these dependencies reduces steering efficacy.
The effect of steering is less significant when the base model's trait expression is already at an extreme (very high or very low).
future_direction: Disentangling trait-specific control from shared semantic structure without degrading steering effectiveness.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models exhibit implicit personalities in their generation, but reliably controlling or aligning these traits to meet specific needs remains an open challenge. The need for effective mechanisms for behavioural manipulation of the model during generation is a critical gap in the literature that needs to be fulfilled. Personality-aware LLMs hold a promising direction towards this objective. However, the relationship between these psychological constructs and their representations within LLMs remains underexplored and requires further investigation. Moreover, it is intriguing to understand and study the use of these representations to steer the models' behaviour.
