papers.title: Net2Vec: Quantifying and Explaining How Concepts are Encoded by Filters in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: To what extent are individual filters sufficient to express a concept, and to what extent are filters shared between concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Net2Vec, a framework for learning concept embeddings aligned to filter activations, and uses it to show that concepts are encoded distributively across multiple filters and that filters are often shared among concepts.
papers.conclusion: Concepts are encoded distributively across filters and filters are shared among concepts; the Net2Vec framework provides a way to quantify and explain these relationships.
papers.key_findings:
Multiple filters are required to code for a concept in most cases.
Filters are not concept-specific and often help encode multiple concepts.
Filter embeddings better characterize the meaning of a representation and its relationship to other concepts compared to single filter activations.
Linear combinations of filters outperform single filters for segmentation and classification tasks.
The number of filters required to encode a concept varies by concept category and task.
papers.limitation:
The approach is limited by its linear nature.
Failure cases occur for concepts with very few training examples or very small objects.
future_direction: Explore non-linear ways concepts can be better aligned to the filter space.
papers.abstract: In an effort to understand the meaning of the intermediate representations captured by deep networks, recent papers have tried to associate specific semantic concepts to individual neural network filter responses, where interesting correlations are often found, largely by focusing on extremal filter responses. In this paper, we show that this approach can favor easy-to-interpret cases that are not necessarily representative of the average behavior of a representation. A more realistic but harder-to-study hypothesis is that semantic representations are distributed, and thus filters must be studied in conjunction. In order to investigate this idea while enabling systematic visualization and quantification of multiple filter responses, we introduce the Net2Vec framework, in which semantic concepts are mapped to vectorial embeddings based on corresponding filter responses. By studying such embeddings, we are able to show that 1., in most cases, multiple filters are required to code for a concept, that 2., often filters are not concept specific and help encode multiple concepts, and that 3., compared to single filter activations, filter embeddings are able to better characterize the meaning of a representation and its relationship to other concepts.

papers.title: Discovering Latent Concepts Learned in BERT
papers.research_question: What latent concepts exist in the pre-trained BERT model, how do the discovered latent concepts align or diverge from classical linguistic hierarchy, and how do the latent concepts evolve across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an unsupervised method to discover and analyze latent concepts learned in BERT, and releases a novel multi-facet hierarchical concept dataset (BCN).
papers.conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive analysis of latent concepts in BERT and releases a novel BERT-centric concept dataset (BCN) that facilitates future interpretation studies and serves as an annotated resource.
papers.key_findings:
BERT learns novel concepts (e.g., animal categories, demographic groups) that do not strictly adhere to pre-defined linguistic categories.
Many latent concepts are based on multiple properties (e.g., semantics, syntax, morphology).
Lower layers dominate in learning shallow lexical concepts, while higher layers learn semantic relations.
The discovered latent concepts highlight potential biases learned in the model (e.g., gender and demographic associations).
Concepts learned at higher layers are more aligned with linguistically motivated concepts compared to lower layers.
papers.limitation:
The diversity of observed concepts is limited by the dataset and clustering constraints (memory and algorithm).
Only the final layer of BERT was manually annotated due to annotation cost.
The method is limited to word-level concepts; phrase-level concepts are not explored.
future_direction: Increase diversity of concepts by working around memory and algorithm constraints.
Explore phrase-level concepts.
Incorporate principal component analysis for more controlled analysis.
papers.abstract: A large number of studies that analyze deep neural network models and their ability to encode various linguistic and non-linguistic concepts provide an interpretation of the inner mechanics of these models. The scope of the analyses is limited to pre-defined concepts that reinforce the traditional linguistic knowledge and do not reflect on how novel concepts are learned by the model. We address this limitation by discovering and analyzing latent concepts learned in neural network models in an unsupervised fashion and provide interpretations from the model's perspective. In this work, we study: i) what latent concepts exist in the pre-trained BERT model, ii) how the discovered latent concepts align or diverge from classical linguistic hierarchy and iii) how the latent concepts evolve across layers. Our findings show: i) a model learns novel concepts (e.g. animal categories and demographic groups), which do not strictly adhere to any pre-defined categorization (e.g. POS, semantic tags), ii) several latent concepts are based on multiple properties which may include semantics, syntax, and morphology, iii) the lower layers in the model dominate in learning shallow lexical concepts while the higher layers learn semantic relations and iv) the discovered latent concepts highlight potential biases learned in the model. We also release a novel BERT ConceptNet dataset (BCN) consisting of 174 concept labels and 1M annotated instances.

papers.title: Word Meanings in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How are word meanings represented in transformer language models? Specifically, do transformer models use a lexical store that encodes semantic information in static token embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: The static token embeddings in transformer language models encode a wide variety of semantic information, supporting the idea that LLMs use a lexical store for word meanings and ruling out meaning eliminativist hypotheses.
papers.conclusion: Static embeddings in transformer models store meaningful semantic information, not just syntactic and surface-level features, indicating LLMs require a lexical store of semantic information for understanding text.
papers.key_findings:
Manual inspection of k-means clusters from RoBERTa-base static embeddings reveals many clusters organized by semantic categories (e.g., colors, tools, medical terms).
Quantitative analysis shows clusters are sensitive to psycholinguistic attributes (valence, concreteness, iconicity, taboo, age of acquisition), indicating semantic information is encoded.
The findings rule out meaning eliminativist hypotheses that static embeddings contain little semantic information.
The static embedding space encodes both taxonomic and thematic relations among words.
Some clusters capture worldly information (e.g., political names, sports teams) in addition to semantic features.
papers.limitation:
The iconicity findings are limited, with only 9 sensitive clusters and no clear iconicity-related features upon manual inspection; iconicity may correlate with surface features like syllable count.
The taboo attribute list is small (1,085 tokens), leading to sampling errors and a small number of sensitive clusters.
Clusters sensitive to an attribute might be sensitive to correlative properties rather than the attribute itself.
future_direction: Using alternative embeddings and clustering algorithms (e.g., variations of the EM algorithm).
Using alternative null hypotheses in statistical tests.
Considering subsets of corpora partitioned by source classifications (e.g., cultural biases, sub-populations, settings) to test for idiosyncratic meanings.
papers.abstract: We investigate how word meanings are represented in the transformer language models. Specifically, we focus on whether transformer models employ something analogous to a lexical store - where each word has an entry that contains semantic information. To do this, we extracted the token embedding space of RoBERTa-base and k-means clustered it into 200 clusters. In our first study, we then manually inspected the resultant clusters to consider whether they are sensitive to semantic information. In our second study, we tested whether the clusters are sensitive to five psycholinguistic measures: valence, concreteness, iconicity, taboo, and age of acquisition. Overall, our findings were very positive - there is a wide variety of semantic information encoded within the token embedding space. This serves to rule out certain "meaning eliminativist" hypotheses about how transformer LLMs process semantic information.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: Discovering Chunks in Neural Embeddings for Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can the cognitive mechanism of chunking be leveraged to interpret high-dimensional neural population activities in artificial neural networks? The paper tests the 'reflection hypothesis' that neural network activities reflect regularities in the data they are trained on.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel interpretability framework that uses the cognitive principle of chunking to identify recurring patterns (chunks) in neural embeddings, showing these chunks reflect data regularities and can causally influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The cognitive tendency for chunking can be leveraged to segment high-dimensional neural activity into recurring, interpretable chunks, revealing a structured reflection of the world within artificial neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
In simple RNNs trained on artificial sequences, hidden states reflect input regularities and can be extracted as interpretable chunks using discrete sequence chunking.
Extracted chunks in RNNs have a causal role: grafting these hidden states alters network predictions and can facilitate compositional learning.
In LLMs (LLaMA3-8B), neural population averaging can extract chunks corresponding to recurring words/concepts, with the extracted subpopulation activity serving as a classifier for the signal.
Unsupervised chunk discovery in LLM embeddings reveals chunks that correlate with abstract concepts like part-of-speech tags, suggesting they capture syntactic information.
The number and diversity of neural population chunks increase with the complexity and hierarchical structure of the input sequence, supporting the reflection hypothesis.
papers.limitation: The approach is an initial proof of concept and has limitations. Future work is needed to test it across different models, establish theoretical foundations, and refine chunk extraction methods.
future_direction: Test the reflection hypothesis across different models.
Establish theoretical foundations for the approach.
Refine chunk extraction methods, such as capturing multi-token chunks in unsupervised discovery.
Extend the framework toward nonparametric chunk discovery.
papers.abstract: Understanding neural networks is challenging due to their high-dimensional, interacting components. Inspired by human cognition, which processes complex sensory data by chunking it into recurring entities, we propose leveraging this principle to interpret artificial neural population activities. Biological and artificial intelligence share the challenge of learning from structured, naturalistic data, and we hypothesize that the cognitive mechanism of chunking can provide insights into artificial systems. We first demonstrate this concept in recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained on artificial sequences with imposed regularities, observing that their hidden states reflect these patterns, which can be extracted as a dictionary of chunks that influence network responses. Extending this to large language models (LLMs) like LLaMA, we identify similar recurring embedding states corresponding to concepts in the input, with perturbations to these states activating or inhibiting the associated concepts. By exploring methods to extract dictionaries of identifiable chunks across neural embeddings of varying complexity, our findings introduce a new framework for interpreting neural networks, framing their population activity as structured reflections of the data they process.

papers.title: Predicting Human Similarity Judgments with Distributional Models: The Value of Word Associations
papers.research_question: Can internal language models (I-language) derived from word associations better predict human similarity judgments compared to external language models (E-language) derived from text corpora?
papers.core_contribution: I-language models based on word associations consistently outperform E-language models based on text corpora in predicting human similarity judgments, suggesting that word associations capture semantic information not fully encoded in text.
papers.conclusion: I-language models based on word associations provide a better approximation to human semantic representations than E-language models, and word associations capture information beyond what is available in text corpora.
papers.key_findings:
I-language models (based on word associations) outperform E-language models (based on text corpora) in predicting human similarity judgments.
The random walk model (I-language) performs best overall.
The count model for word associations (PMI+) also performs well, sometimes outperforming word2vec on certain tasks (e.g., remote triads).
The performance of I-language models is achieved with much less data than E-language models.
The results suggest that human similarity judgments rely more on semantic associations than on distributional patterns in text.
future_direction: Incorporate perceptual and emotional information to improve E-language models.
papers.abstract: To represent the meaning of a word, most models use external language resources, such as text corpora, to derive the distributional properties of word usage. In this study, we propose that internal language models, that are more closely aligned to the mental representations of words, can be used to derive new theoretical questions regarding the structure of the mental lexicon. A comparison with internal models also puts into perspective a number of assumptions underlying recently proposed distributional text-based models could provide important insights into cognitive science, including linguistics and artificial intelligence. We focus on word-embedding models which have been proposed to learn aspects of word meaning in a manner similar to humans and contrast them with internal language models derived from a new extensive data set of word associations. An evaluation using relatedness judgments shows that internal language models consistently outperform current state-of-the art text-based external language models. This suggests alternative approaches to represent word meaning using properties that aren't encoded in text.

papers.title: Making Sense of CNNs: Interpreting Deep Representations & Their Invariances with INNs
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the deep representations learned by neural networks and the invariances they capture, to make black-box models more understandable?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an invertible neural network (INN) based approach that recovers the invariances learned by a deep model and transforms its representations into an interpretable space with accessible semantic concepts, without modifying the original model.
papers.conclusion: The proposed invertible approach provides a comprehensive diagnostic pipeline for explaining deep representations by recovering their invariances and translating them into semantically accessible concepts.
papers.key_findings:
The method produces higher quality visualizations of network representations across layers compared to existing inversion methods, as measured by lower FID scores.
Analysis of FaceNet reveals that it uses glasses as an identity feature throughout all layers, indicating a bias.
Tracking semantic concept relevance during training shows that a classifier learns to focus on task-relevant attributes (e.g., digit shape) and ignore irrelevant ones (e.g., color).
Visualizing representations of adversarially attacked images shows how the attack propagates through the network, with vulnerability correlated to the amount of invariance in a layer.
The approach validates the texture-bias hypothesis in CNNs, showing a standard ImageNet-trained ResNet focuses on texture, while one trained on stylized ImageNet focuses on shape.
papers.abstract: To tackle increasingly complex tasks, it has become an essential ability of neural networks to learn abstract representations. These task-specific representations and, particularly, the invariances they capture turn neural networks into black box models that lack interpretability. To open such a black box, it is, therefore, crucial to uncover the different semantic concepts a model has learned as well as those that it has learned to be invariant to. We present an approach based on INNs that (i) recovers the task-specific, learned invariances by disentangling the remaining factor of variation in the data and that (ii) invertibly transforms these recovered invariances combined with the model representation into an equally expressive one with accessible semantic concepts. As a consequence, neural network representations become understandable by providing the means to (i) expose their semantic meaning, (ii) semantically modify a representation, and (iii) visualize individual learned semantic concepts and invariances. Our invertible approach significantly extends the abilities to understand black box models by enabling post-hoc interpretations of state-of-the-art networks without compromising their performance. Our implementation is available at https://compvis.github.io/invariances/ .

papers.title: Saliency Suppressed, Semantics Surfaced: Visual Transformations in Neural Networks and the Brain
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode low-level (visual saliency) and high-level (semantic similarity) information, and how do these representations compare to those in the human visual cortex?
papers.core_contribution: ResNets are more sensitive to saliency than ViTs, and suppress saliency in early layers (enhanced by CLIP training). CLIP enhances semantic encoding in both architectures. Semantic encoding drives alignment with human visual perception, while saliency suppression is a non-brain-like strategy.
papers.conclusion: Semantic encoding is a primary driver of alignment between neural network representations and the human visual cortex, while the strategy of suppressing salient visual information is unique to artificial networks and not observed in human visual processing.
papers.key_findings:
ResNets are more sensitive to saliency information than Vision Transformers (ViTs) when trained with object classification objectives.
ResNets suppress saliency information in early layers, a process enhanced by natural language supervision (CLIP).
CLIP training enhances semantic encoding in both ResNet and ViT architectures.
Semantic encoding is a key factor in aligning artificial neural network representations with human visual cortex representations, while saliency suppression is not observed in the brain.
ViTs are less sensitive to salient distractors than ResNets, and CLIP reduces the additive effect of saliency on semantic disturbance in ResNets.
papers.limitation:
The analysis of CLIP's impact is limited by its training on a larger and more diverse dataset compared to ImageNet, making it unclear if effects are due to language supervision or exposure to complex visual scenes.
fMRI may have limitations in capturing early visual processes critical for saliency, potentially affecting the measured alignment between saliency and cortical activity.
future_direction: Circuit-level analyses to understand saliency suppression.
Establishing formal links between saliency maps and CNN computations.
Assessing neural network responses to a variety of low-to-mid-level image descriptors beyond saliency.
papers.abstract: Deep learning algorithms lack human-interpretable accounts of how they transform raw visual input into a robust semantic understanding, which impedes comparisons between different architectures, training objectives, and the human brain. In this work, we take inspiration from neuroscience and employ representational approaches to shed light on how neural networks encode information at low (visual saliency) and high (semantic similarity) levels of abstraction. Moreover, we introduce a custom image dataset where we systematically manipulate salient and semantic information. We find that ResNets are more sensitive to saliency information than ViTs, when trained with object classification objectives. We uncover that networks suppress saliency in early layers, a process enhanced by natural language supervision (CLIP) in ResNets. CLIP also enhances semantic encoding in both architectures. Finally, we show that semantic encoding is a key factor in aligning AI with human visual perception, while saliency suppression is a non-brain-like strategy.

papers.title: Prediction is not Explanation: Revisiting the Explanatory Capacity of Mapping Embeddings
papers.research_question: Does prediction accuracy in mapping word embeddings to feature norms reliably indicate genuine feature-based interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that prediction accuracy in property inference methods does not reliably indicate genuine feature-based interpretability, as the results are largely determined by methodological upper bounds and geometric similarity rather than information overlap.
papers.conclusion: Property inference methods do not provide faithful explanations of emergent feature knowledge in word embeddings; instead, they reflect geometric similarities and are limited by methodological constraints.
papers.key_findings:
Property inference methods (PLSR and FFNN) are essentially equivalent when hyperparameters are tuned properly.
The upper bound for perfect information overlap is very low for sparse feature norms, and prediction accuracy is close to this bound.
Random features can be predicted to some degree, and it is not distinguishable whether the result is limited by information overlap or the upper bound.
Corrupting essential linguistic features (like hypernyms) does not significantly change prediction results.
Mapping embeddings to feature norms captures geometric similarity between the matrices, not individual properties.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to three specific feature norms and BERT embeddings.
The study does not explore other property inference algorithms beyond PLSR and FFNN.
future_direction: Analyze the dependence of explanatory power on sparsity, geometric structures, and properties of scores.
Investigate under which circumstances emerging property knowledge could be analyzed with inference methods.
papers.abstract: Understanding what knowledge is implicitly encoded in deep learning models is essential for improving the interpretability of AI systems. This paper examines common methods to explain the knowledge encoded in word embeddings, which are core elements of large language models (LLMs). These methods typically involve mapping embeddings onto collections of human-interpretable semantic features, known as feature norms. Prior work assumes that accurately predicting these semantic features from the word embeddings implies that the embeddings contain the corresponding knowledge. We challenge this assumption by demonstrating that prediction accuracy alone does not reliably indicate genuine feature-based interpretability. We show that these methods can successfully predict even random information, concluding that the results are predominantly determined by an algorithmic upper bound rather than meaningful semantic representation in the word embeddings. Consequently, comparisons between datasets based solely on prediction performance do not reliably indicate which dataset is better captured by the word embeddings. Our analysis illustrates that such mappings primarily reflect geometric similarity within vector spaces rather than indicating the genuine emergence of semantic properties.

papers.title: The Representation and Recall of Interwoven Structured Knowledge in LLMs: A Geometric and Layered Analysis
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode interwoven scientific knowledge, and do they reflect geometric structures like the periodic table?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode scientific knowledge in geometric structures, such as a 3D spiral aligning with the periodic table, representing knowledge as interwoven manifolds rather than isolated facts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop internal representations that reflect the structured geometry of scientific knowledge, representing symbolic knowledge as geometry-aware, interwoven manifolds.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure is observed in hidden states that aligns with the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous attributes enabling indirect recall, while deeper layers sharpen categorical distinctions.
Linguistic context increasingly shapes representations in later layers.
Middle layers have strong linear associations between related attributes, which weaken in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Prompts are focused on chemical elements and may not extend to domains with more abstract features.
Hypothesis-driven validation may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge, such as materials property prediction.
Informing the design of downstream embedding-based tasks.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how large language models (LLMs) represent and recall multi-associated attributes across transformer layers. We show that intermediate layers encode factual knowledge by superimposing related attributes in overlapping spaces, along with effective recall even when attributes are not explicitly prompted. In contrast, later layers refine linguistic patterns and progressively separate attribute representations, optimizing task-specific outputs while appropriately narrowing attribute recall. We identify diverse encoding patterns including, for the first time, the observation of 3D spiral structures when exploring information related to the periodic table of elements. Our findings reveal a dynamic transition in attribute representations across layers, contributing to mechanistic interpretability and providing insights for understanding how LLMs handle complex, interrelated knowledge.

papers.title: Interpreting Key Mechanisms of Factual Recall in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based language models perform factual recall, specifically how do they extract arguments from context and apply implicit functions through MLPs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a detailed mechanistic interpretation of factual recall in transformers, introducing a method to decompose MLP outputs and identifying a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer.
papers.conclusion: The paper outlines a pipeline for factual recall in transformers, proposes a novel analytic method for MLPs, and identifies a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism that can be mitigated to improve factual recall confidence.
papers.key_findings:
Task-specific attention heads extract topic tokens and pass them to subsequent MLPs.
MLPs act as activations that amplify or erase individual attention head outputs in the residual stream.
Deep MLPs apply implicit functions by adding a task-aware component that redirects the residual stream towards the correct answer.
A universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer suppresses correct predictions, which can be mitigated using the proposed interpretation.
These mechanisms are consistent across models (GPT-2, OPT, Llama-2), tasks (country-capital, product-developer), and few-shot settings.
papers.limitation:
The paper does not explore how the model constructs task semantics within its shallow layers.
The origins of the identified mechanisms (e.g., why MLPs redirect the residual stream) need further research.
The proposed analysis method for decomposing MLP outputs requires preliminary human reasoning and is not fully automated.
future_direction: Exploring how task semantics are constructed in shallow layers through collaborative circuit paths.
Investigating the origins of the mechanisms, such as why MLP outputs are structured as y-x.
Developing more automated interpretation techniques for MLPs.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we delve into several mechanisms employed by Transformer-based language models (LLMs) for factual recall tasks. We outline a pipeline consisting of three major steps: (1) Given a prompt ``The capital of France is,'' task-specific attention heads extract the topic token, such as ``France,'' from the context and pass it to subsequent MLPs. (2) As attention heads' outputs are aggregated with equal weight and added to the residual stream, the subsequent MLP acts as an ``activation,'' which either erases or amplifies the information originating from individual heads. As a result, the topic token ``France'' stands out in the residual stream. (3) A deep MLP takes ``France'' and generates a component that redirects the residual stream towards the direction of the correct answer, i.e., ``Paris.'' This procedure is akin to applying an implicit function such as ``get\_capital($X$),'' and the argument $X$ is the topic token information passed by attention heads. To achieve the above quantitative and qualitative analysis for MLPs, we proposed a novel analytic method aimed at decomposing the outputs of the MLP into components understandable by humans. Additionally, we observed a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer of models, which suppresses correct predictions. We mitigate this suppression by leveraging our interpretation to improve factual recall confidence. The above interpretations are evaluated across diverse tasks spanning various domains of factual knowledge, using various language models from the GPT-2 families, 1.3B OPT, up to 7B Llama-2, and in both zero- and few-shot setups.

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Language Models Are Specific to Human Language
papers.research_question: Are correlations between language model hidden states and fMRI brain responses robust to dimensionality concerns, and are they specific to models trained on human language and dependent on positional encoding?
papers.core_contribution: The study confirms that correlations between transformer language model hidden states and human brain activity during language tasks are robust, specific to language-trained models, and heavily dependent on positional encodings.
papers.conclusion: The internal representations of transformer language models are strongly correlated with human brain activity during language processing, and this alignment is specific to language-trained models and relies on positional information.
papers.key_findings:
Removing positional encodings significantly reduces brain-model correlations and distorts the geometric similarity between model and brain representational spaces.
Dimensionality reduction via PCA does not eliminate the correlations, indicating they are not an artifact of the curse of dimensionality.
Models trained on non-linguistic data (protein sequences) show negligible alignment with brain activity, confirming the language-specificity of the effects.
Causal (decoder-only) language models show higher alignment with brain activity than bidirectional models.
The geometric structure of model and brain representations, measured by CKA and Gromov-Wasserstein distance, is similar and degrades when positional information is removed.
papers.limitation:
The dataset includes only 243 stimuli and 6 subjects, limiting statistical power and generalizability.
The head-wise analysis pooled voxels across cortical regions without distinguishing between different regions of interest.
The study uses text-only models and fMRI data from reading tasks; future work should use modality-matched datasets (e.g., audio models with spoken language tasks).
future_direction: Increase the number of subjects and model diversity to improve statistical power and generalizability.
Conduct finer-grained region-of-interest (ROI) by head analysis to reveal differential alignment patterns.
Use modality-matched datasets (e.g., spoken-language tasks with audio models) to disentangle task effects from representational differences.
papers.abstract: Previous work has shown correlations between the hidden states of large language models and fMRI brain responses, on language tasks. These correlations have been taken as evidence of the representational similarity of these models and brain states. This study tests whether these previous results are robust to several possible concerns. Specifically this study shows: (i) that the previous results are still found after dimensionality reduction, and thus are not attributable to the curse of dimensionality; (ii) that previous results are confirmed when using new measures of similarity; (iii) that correlations between brain representations and those from models are specific to models trained on human language; and (iv) that the results are dependent on the presence of positional encoding in the models. These results confirm and strengthen the results of previous research and contribute to the debate on the biological plausibility and interpretability of state-of-the-art large language models.

papers.title: Beyond Single Concept Vector: Modeling Concept Subspace in LLMs with Gaussian Distribution
papers.research_question: Instead of using a single vector to describe each underlying concept captured by LLMs, can we use a distribution (specifically a Gaussian distribution) to more robustly describe that learned concept?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Gaussian Concept Subspace (GCS), a method to represent concepts in LLMs as a Gaussian distribution of vectors, which is more robust than single vectors and effective for concept representation and emotion steering.
papers.conclusion: GCS offers a concise yet powerful method for concept subspace estimation, showing promise in both theoretical explanations and practical applications.
papers.key_findings:
GCS-sampled concept vectors are faithful and plausible, showing high similarity to observed vectors and comparable or better accuracy.
GCS reveals hierarchical concept structures that align with human understanding.
GCS vectors are effective in inference-time intervention for emotion steering, balancing steering performance and fluency.
Sampled vectors within 1σ and 2σ achieve better prediction accuracy than observed vectors.
The method is robust across different model architectures and sizes (Llama-2-7B, Gemma-7B, Llama-2-13B).
papers.limitation: Evaluating GCS at the distribution level is challenging due to the infinite potential of sampled vectors and the variability in relevance with distance from the mean.
papers.abstract: Probing learned concepts in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for understanding how semantic knowledge is encoded internally. Training linear classifiers on probing tasks is a principle approach to denote the vector of a certain concept in the representation space. However, the single vector identified for a concept varies with both data and training, making it less robust and weakening its effectiveness in real-world applications. To address this challenge, we propose an approach to approximate the subspace representing a specific concept. Built on linear probing classifiers, we extend the concept vectors into Gaussian Concept Subspace (GCS). We demonstrate GCS's effectiveness through measuring its faithfulness and plausibility across multiple LLMs with different sizes and architectures. Additionally, we use representation intervention tasks to showcase its efficacy in real-world applications such as emotion steering. Experimental results indicate that GCS concept vectors have the potential to balance steering performance and maintaining the fluency in natural language generation tasks.

papers.title: Self-StrAE at SemEval-2024 Task 1: Making Self-Structuring AutoEncoders Learn More With Less
papers.research_question: How can Self-Structuring AutoEncoder (Self-StrAE) be improved to learn embeddings that capture semantic relatedness, especially in low-resource settings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that adding a discrete reconstruction objective and increasing the number of independent channels in Self-StrAE improves its performance on semantic relatedness tasks while reducing the number of non-embedding parameters, and shows effectiveness across multiple languages with limited pre-training data.
papers.conclusion: The improvements to Self-StrAE demonstrate the promise of inductive biases towards explicit structure in learning embeddings, and with further refinements, such models could be valuable for low-resource languages where data is scarce.
papers.key_findings:
Combining cross entropy and contrastive loss (CECO) leads to better representations than using each objective individually.
Increasing the number of independent channels while decreasing their size improves embedding quality and reduces parameters, but can cause training instability.
The model can be pre-trained from scratch with as little as 10M tokens and performs well on semantic relatedness tasks.
The improvements hold across English, Spanish, and Afrikaans, with comparable or better performance.
A proposed solution (StrCSE) helps stabilize training with high channel counts, though further analysis is needed.
papers.limitation:
The cause of training instability when the number of channels is increased is not fully understood.
The performance evaluation is limited to Indo-European languages (English, Spanish, Afrikaans), and it's unclear how it generalizes to other languages.
future_direction: Investigating a broader spectrum of languages beyond Indo-European languages.
Further analysis to understand the causes of training instability with increased channels.
Pursuing further refinements to the model to achieve more substantial benefits.
papers.abstract: This paper presents two simple improvements to the Self-Structuring AutoEncoder (Self-StrAE). Firstly, we show that including reconstruction to the vocabulary as an auxiliary objective improves representation quality. Secondly, we demonstrate that increasing the number of independent channels leads to significant improvements in embedding quality, while simultaneously reducing the number of parameters. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that this trend can be followed to the extreme, even to point of reducing the total number of non-embedding parameters to seven. Our system can be pre-trained from scratch with as little as 10M tokens of input data, and proves effective across English, Spanish and Afrikaans.

papers.title: Discovering Salient Neurons in Deep NLP Models
papers.research_question: Can we identify subsets of neurons that learn specific linguistic properties, and how is linguistic knowledge localized, distributed, and affected by fine-tuning in NLP models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Linguistic Correlation Analysis (LCA) for extracting salient neurons in NLP models, revealing that linguistic knowledge is localized in lower layers for basic properties and distributed in higher layers for complex concepts, with variations across models and during fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The LCA method provides insights into how linguistic knowledge is encoded in neurons, showing localization patterns and redistribution during fine-tuning, with implications for model understanding and transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Small subsets of neurons can predict different linguistic tasks.
Neurons for basic lexical information are localized in lower layers, while those for complex concepts are in higher layers.
Linguistic information is redundantly preserved across neurons.
During transfer learning, salient linguistic neurons relocate to lower layers in some models like RoBERTa and XLNet.
Multilingual models exhibit similar neuron distribution for concepts across different languages.
future_direction: Pinpointing specific concepts regressed to lower layers versus those retained in higher layers during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: While a lot of work has been done in understanding representations learned within deep NLP models and what knowledge they capture, little attention has been paid towards individual neurons. We present a technique called as Linguistic Correlation Analysis to extract salient neurons in the model, with respect to any extrinsic property - with the goal of understanding how such a knowledge is preserved within neurons. We carry out a fine-grained analysis to answer the following questions: (i) can we identify subsets of neurons in the network that capture specific linguistic properties? (ii) how localized or distributed neurons are across the network? iii) how redundantly is the information preserved? iv) how fine-tuning pre-trained models towards downstream NLP tasks, impacts the learned linguistic knowledge? iv) how do architectures vary in learning different linguistic properties? Our data-driven, quantitative analysis illuminates interesting findings: (i) we found small subsets of neurons that can predict different linguistic tasks, ii) with neurons capturing basic lexical information (such as suffixation) localized in lower most layers, iii) while those learning complex concepts (such as syntactic role) predominantly in middle and higher layers, iii) that salient linguistic neurons are relocated from higher to lower layers during transfer learning, as the network preserve the higher layers for task specific information, iv) we found interesting differences across pre-trained models, with respect to how linguistic information is preserved within, and v) we found that concept exhibit similar neuron distribution across different languages in the multilingual transformer models. Our code is publicly available as part of the NeuroX toolkit.

papers.title: Representation and Pre-Activation of Lexical-Semantic Knowledge in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How closely do the intermediate layers of LSTM and transformer language models correspond to human semantic knowledge, both before and after the target word is presented?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer models (GPT-2) are better at capturing semantic knowledge, especially attributive features, than LSTM models, and both models retain rich semantic representations of a concept after it has been presented.
papers.conclusion: The transformer model is much better at capturing attributive features than the LSTM model, whilst both models are able to retain rich semantic representations of the concept after the concept has been given to the network.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer models (GPT-2) outperform LSTM models in capturing semantic knowledge, particularly for attributive features.
Both models retain semantic information about a concept after the word is presented, with earlier layers performing better in the 'after' condition.
The final layer of both models shows a performance drop in the 'after' condition, likely due to increased context specificity.
In the 'before' condition (predicting the word), later layers are more representative of the upcoming word's semantics.
GPT-2's after representations are more effective in lower layers, while JLM's after representations are better in the first layer.
papers.limitation:
The feature pooling method may not fully capture context-specific representations, especially in later layers where representations become more context-specific.
Linear probes may not fully capture the information encoded in the representations; failure to decode a property does not mean it is not encoded.
papers.abstract: Neural network language models have the ability to capture the contextualised meanings of words in a sentence by dynamically evolving a representation of the linguistic input in a manner evocative of human language comprehension. While researchers have been able to analyse whether key linguistic regularities are adequately characterised by these evolving representations, determining whether they activate lexico-semantic knowledge similarly to humans remains challenging. In this paper, we perform a systematic analysis of how closely the intermediate layers from LSTM and transformer language models correspond to human semantic knowledge. Furthermore, in order to make more meaningful comparisons with theories of human language comprehension in psycholinguistics, we focus on two key stages where the meaning of a particular target word may arise: immediately before the word's presentation to the model (comparable to forward inferencing), and immediately after the word token has been input into the network. Our results indicate that the transformer models are better at capturing semantic knowledge relating to lexical concepts, both during word prediction and when retention is required.

papers.title: Concept-Based Mechanistic Interpretability Using Structured Knowledge Graphs
papers.research_question: How can concept-based interpretability methods be extended to provide a global, mechanistic understanding of how semantic concepts emerge, interact, and propagate through a model's internal components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BAGEL, a scalable framework and interactive tool for global, concept-based mechanistic interpretability that models how semantic concepts are represented and interact across a model's internal layers, enabling systematic analysis of bias alignment between datasets and models.
papers.conclusion: BAGEL offers a global perspective for dissecting concept-based biases in DNNs, bridging the gap between dataset-driven and model-learned concept representations to provide deeper insight into model decision-making processes.
papers.key_findings:
BAGEL provides a global view of concept distributions and their alignment with external semantic priors, bridging dataset-driven and model-learned concept representations.
Early network layers tend to mix concepts with limited class relevance, while deeper layers filter and emphasize concepts more aligned with the input class.
The method can identify spurious correlations and model-specific biases not present in the dataset, visualized via an interactive knowledge graph.
BAGEL demonstrates strong and consistent performance in detecting dataset biases compared to baseline methods like TCAV and SAE.
Rudimentary concepts (e.g., materials, textures) manifest in initial layers, while deeper layers show higher probabilities for more complex concepts (e.g., object parts).
papers.limitation: The logistic regression classifiers used for concept prediction assume a linear relation between features and concepts, which may limit the ability to capture more complex patterns.
future_direction: Extending BAGEL to multimodal architectures.
Refining concept definitions through automated discovery.
papers.abstract: While concept-based interpretability methods have traditionally focused on local explanations of neural network predictions, we propose a novel framework and interactive tool that extends these methods into the domain of mechanistic interpretability. Our approach enables a global dissection of model behavior by analyzing how high-level semantic attributes (referred to as concepts) emerge, interact, and propagate through internal model components. Unlike prior work that isolates individual neurons or predictions, our framework systematically quantifies how semantic concepts are represented across layers, revealing latent circuits and information flow that underlie model decision-making. A key innovation is our visualization platform that we named BAGEL (for Bias Analysis with a Graph for global Explanation Layers), which presents these insights in a structured knowledge graph, allowing users to explore concept-class relationships, identify spurious correlations, and enhance model trustworthiness. Our framework is model-agnostic, scalable, and contributes to a deeper understanding of how deep learning models generalize (or fail to) in the presence of dataset biases. The demonstration is available at https://knowledge-graph-ui-4a7cb5.gitlab.io/.

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How do different strategies for extracting lexical type-level knowledge from pretrained language models impact performance across languages and tasks? Is lexical knowledge concentrated in few parameters or scattered? How do these representations compare to traditional static word vectors? Do monolingual LMs learn similar representations for translation pairs?
papers.core_contribution: A systematic study of how to extract lexical type-level knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that lexical information is concentrated in lower layers and that extracted representations can outperform traditional static word embeddings in some tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effective extraction depends on configuration choices such as using monolingual LMs, averaging over lower layers, and excluding special tokens.
papers.key_findings:
Monolingual LMs contain more lexical information than multilingual LMs.
Lexical information is concentrated in lower Transformer layers.
Averaging over multiple layers (especially lower ones) yields better representations than single layers.
Excluding special tokens [CLS] and [SEP] improves performance.
Extracted representations can outperform fastText in monolingual tasks but underperform in cross-lingual tasks.
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect AOC configurations and sampling representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, tasks, and larger underlying LMs.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods (e.g., layer weighting or attention).
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-of-context versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: Finding Shared Decodable Concepts and their Negations in the Brain
papers.research_question: How can we identify shared decodable concepts (SDCs) in the brain from fMRI data during natural image viewing? The paper proposes a method using contrastive learning and a novel clustering approach to find voxel clusters across participants that represent similar semantic concepts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using contrastive learning and a novel cross-participant DBSCAN clustering to identify shared decodable concepts (SDCs) in the brain from fMRI data, revealing both known and new visuo-semantic categories.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method successfully identifies shared decodable concepts in the brain, including both previously reported and novel visuo-semantic categories, and the use of negative images aids in interpreting the semantic properties of each cluster.
papers.key_findings:
Identified SDCs for known visual features (e.g., orientation tuning in early visual cortex) and semantic concepts (faces, places, bodies).
Discovered two distinct food-related clusters: one driven by color and another by shape, with negative images revealing grayscale images for the color-driven cluster.
Found body-related clusters for legs/hands, motion, and groups of people in extrastriate body area (EBA).
Discovered a numerosity cluster in right intraparietal sulcus (IPS) associated with repeated elements.
Identified clusters for visual perspective (close/far) and lighting conditions.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the stimulus images used in the NSD experiment, which may bias the model towards over-represented categories.
The use of CLIP may introduce biases, as some brain signal may not be captured by CLIP embeddings.
fMRI has limited temporal resolution, restricting the ability to capture rapid neural activity.
The clustering approach might merge concepts within regions of CLIP space that have relatively uniform densities, potentially missing interesting SDCs.
The method is not a replacement for traditional hypothesis-driven experiments.
future_direction: Utilize larger and more diverse fMRI datasets.
Incorporate higher temporal resolution imaging techniques such as EEG or ECoG.
Explore alternative stimulus representations beyond CLIP.
papers.abstract: Prior work has offered evidence for functional localization in the brain; different anatomical regions preferentially activate for certain types of visual input. For example, the fusiform face area preferentially activates for visual stimuli that include a face. However, the spectrum of visual semantics is extensive, and only a few semantically-tuned patches of cortex have so far been identified in the human brain. Using a multimodal (natural language and image) neural network architecture (CLIP) we train a highly accurate contrastive model that maps brain responses during naturalistic image viewing to CLIP embeddings. We then use a novel adaptation of the DBSCAN clustering algorithm to cluster the parameters of these participant-specific contrastive models. This reveals what we call Shared Decodable Concepts (SDCs): clusters in CLIP space that are decodable from common sets of voxels across multiple participants. Examining the images most and least associated with each SDC cluster gives us additional insight into the semantic properties of each SDC. We note SDCs for previously reported visual features (e.g. orientation tuning in early visual cortex) as well as visual semantic concepts such as faces, places and bodies. In cases where our method finds multiple clusters for a visuo-semantic concept, the least associated images allow us to dissociate between confounding factors. For example, we discovered two clusters of food images, one driven by color, the other by shape. We also uncover previously unreported areas such as regions of extrastriate body area (EBA) tuned for legs/hands and sensitivity to numerosity in right intraparietal sulcus, and more. Thus, our contrastive-learning methodology better characterizes new and existing visuo-semantic representations in the brain by leveraging multimodal neural network representations and a novel adaptation of clustering algorithms.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: A framework for the emergence and analysis of language in social learning agents
papers.research_question: How are internal representations structured and optimized for communication between agents in social learning, and how does language emerge from such interactions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a teacher-student reinforcement learning framework with a sparse autoencoder to study emergent communication, showing that student feedback shapes the language embedding to prioritize policy information, improving task performance and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides insights into how language emerges from social interactions and how communication constraints shape internal representations, with implications for generalization in cooperative multi-agent systems.
papers.key_findings:
Providing teacher information to the student leads to higher task completion rates and the ability to generalize to unseen tasks.
Optimizing message content with student feedback improves information encoding, altering the latent structure to focus on policy (goal location and initial action) rather than state space (wall position).
The emergent communication exhibits properties of natural language such as compositionality (topographic similarity) and pressure towards entropy minimization.
Feeding back the student's own task information (closing-the-loop) retains some task-relevant information but results in degraded performance and loss of generalization to unknown goals.
Bi-directional communication (with feedback) is critical for transmitting helpful information and enhances the reconstruction capability of the autoencoder.
future_direction: Understanding how social agents reconcile abstractions from their own experience with those acquired through communication.
Achieving a balance between tutoring and learning in multi-task and multi-agent systems to maintain a relevant and generalizable message space.
papers.abstract: Neural systems have evolved not only to solve environmental challenges through internal representations but also, under social constraints, to communicate these to conspecifics. In this work, we aim to understand the structure of these internal representations and how they may be optimized to transmit pertinent information from one individual to another. Thus, we build on previous teacher-student communication protocols to analyze the formation of individual and shared abstractions and their impact on task performance. We use reinforcement learning in grid-world mazes where a teacher network passes a message to a student to improve task performance. This framework allows us to relate environmental variables with individual and shared representations. We compress high-dimensional task information within a low-dimensional representational space to mimic natural language features. In coherence with previous results, we find that providing teacher information to the student leads to a higher task completion rate and an ability to generalize tasks it has not seen before. Further, optimizing message content to maximize student reward improves information encoding, suggesting that an accurate representation in the space of messages requires bi-directional input. These results highlight the role of language as a common representation among agents and its implications on generalization capabilities.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: VISTA: A Panoramic View of Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How to visually explore and interpret neural network representations by mapping them into semantic 2D spaces to uncover patterns and relationships?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces VISTA, a visualization pipeline that uses clustering and text-to-image models to create semantic 2D maps of neural representations, enabling interactive exploration and interpretation.
papers.conclusion: VISTA provides a visual, interactive method for interpreting neural representations that complements automated techniques and offers deeper insights into model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
VISTA confirms automated interpretations from LLM-based methods, validating its basic functionality.
VISTA discovers additional patterns not captured by automated methods, such as secondary triggers for certain latents.
VISTA reveals unexpected associations in latents, highlighting potential limitations in current automated techniques.
papers.limitation: Potential domain skew between datasets or limitations in automated techniques may affect interpretation, as seen in case study 3.
future_direction: Applying VISTA to a broader range of neural representations and integrating it with existing interpretability pipelines.
papers.abstract: We present VISTA (Visualization of Internal States and Their Associations), a novel pipeline for visually exploring and interpreting neural network representations. VISTA addresses the challenge of analyzing vast multidimensional spaces in modern machine learning models by mapping representations into a semantic 2D space. The resulting collages visually reveal patterns and relationships within internal representations. We demonstrate VISTA's utility by applying it to sparse autoencoder latents uncovering new properties and interpretations. We review the VISTA methodology, present findings from our case study ( https://got.drib.net/latents/ ), and discuss implications for neural network interpretability across various domains of machine learning.

papers.title: Representational models: A common framework for understanding encoding, pattern-component, and representational-similarity analysis
papers.research_question: How do encoding analysis, pattern component modeling (PCM), and representational similarity analysis (RSA) relate to each other, and what is their relative power for adjudicating between competing representational models of neural activity?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a common mathematical framework showing that encoding analysis, pattern component modeling (PCM), and representational similarity analysis (RSA) all evaluate the second moment of the distribution of neural activity profiles, which determines representational geometry and feature decodability.
papers.conclusion: Encoding analysis, PCM, and RSA are closely related methods that test hypotheses about the distribution of neural activity profiles and should be considered complementary components of a unified analytical framework for understanding neural representations.
papers.key_findings:
Pattern component modeling (PCM) implements a likelihood-ratio test and provides the most powerful test between representational models if its assumptions hold.
Encoding analysis, when appropriately regularized (effectively imposing a prior on activity profiles), can perform similarly to PCM.
Representational similarity analysis (RSA) can achieve near-optimal inference power when the unequal variances and statistical dependencies of dissimilarity estimates are properly accounted for.
The three methods are complementary: PCM is analytically tractable and powerful, RSA provides intuitive summary statistics, and encoding analysis enables voxel-wise mapping of features.
All three methods are properly construed as components of a single toolkit for testing hypotheses about neural representations.
papers.limitation:
The methods focus on the second moment of the activity profile distribution; higher-order moments, which may be important for distinguishing between population codes with the same decodability, are not considered.
The framework is based on observational data and does not test causal effects of activity patterns on downstream neural or behavioral responses.
future_direction: Investigating the presence and computational function of non-Gaussian distributions of activity profiles in fMRI or single-cell data.
Extending the framework to include free parameters that change the model structure and to incorporate more detailed measurement models for indirect brain activity measures.
papers.abstract: Representational models specify how activity patterns in populations of neurons (or, more generally, in multivariate brain-activity measurements) relate to sensory stimuli, motor responses, or cognitive processes. In an experimental context, representational models can be defined as hypotheses about the distribution of activity profiles across experimental conditions. Currently, three different methods are being used to test such hypotheses: encoding analysis, pattern component modeling (PCM), and representational similarity analysis (RSA). Here we develop a common mathematical framework for understanding the relationship of these three methods, which share one core commonality: all three evaluate the second moment of the distribution of activity profiles, which determines the representational geometry, and thus how well any feature can be decoded from population activity. Using simulated data for three different experimental designs, we compare the power of the methods to adjudicate between competing representational models. PCM implements a likelihood-ratio test and therefore provides the most powerful test if its assumptions hold. However, the other two approaches-when conducted appropriately-can perform similarly. In encoding analysis, the linear model needs to be appropriately regularized, which effectively imposes a prior on the activity profiles. With such a prior, an encoding model specifies a well-defined distribution of activity profiles. In RSA, the unequal variances and statistical dependencies of the dissimilarity estimates need to be taken into account to reach near-optimal power in inference. The three methods render different aspects of the information explicit (e.g. single-response tuning in encoding analysis and population-response representational dissimilarity in RSA) and have specific advantages in terms of computational demands, ease of use, and extensibility. The three methods are properly construed as complementary components of a single data-analytical toolkit for understanding neural representations on the basis of multivariate brain-activity data.

papers.title: Probing for semantic evidence of composition by means of simple classification tasks
papers.research_question: How can we assess whether sentence-level vector representations capture specific semantic information through composition?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a diagnostic method using targeted classification tasks to probe for specific semantic information in sentence representations, aiming to evaluate composition effectiveness.
papers.conclusion: The diagnostic method provides a targeted way to assess semantic information in sentence representations, with potential for broader application and improvement in dataset construction.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve 100% accuracy on lexical presence tasks (e.g., detecting the word 'school').
On semantic role tasks, Skip-Thought embeddings perform well (91.15% accuracy) while averaging-based models (GloVe, Paragram) perform at chance level, indicating the importance of order information.
The method allows for targeted assessment of semantic information like semantic roles and negation scope in composed sentence representations.
papers.limitation:
Automated sentence generation cannot control for plausibility of generated sentences.
Learning low-dimensional vector representations requires a trade-off between coverage and accessibility of encoded information.
future_direction: Developing a broad-coverage suite of classification tasks for comprehensive assessment of semantic information.
Improving dataset construction with more syntactic variation and plausibility annotation.
papers.abstract: We propose a diagnostic method for probing specific information captured in vector representations of sentence meaning, via simple classification tasks with strategically constructed sentence sets. We identify some key types of semantic information that we might expect to be captured in sentence composition, and illustrate example classification tasks for targeting this information.

papers.title: Prompt-Guided Internal States for Hallucination Detection of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we enhance the cross-domain performance of supervised detectors with only in-domain data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PRISM, a framework that uses prompt-guided internal states to enhance the cross-domain generalization of hallucination detectors by making truthfulness structure more salient and consistent.
papers.conclusion: Suitable prompts enhance the salience and consistency of truthfulness structure in LLMs' internal states, and PRISM improves the generalization performance of hallucination detectors.
papers.key_findings:
Introduction of prompts makes the structure related to text truthfulness more salient in LLMs' internal states.
Prompts increase the consistency of truthfulness structure across different domains.
PRISM significantly improves the generalization performance of existing hallucination detection methods.
Variance ratio can effectively guide prompt selection for better performance.
The framework is effective even in real-world scenarios like the TruthfulQA dataset.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on internal states which may be challenging to access, requiring proxy models.
Does not leverage other information like probability information and generated text.
future_direction: Exploring fully utilizing various types of information produced by LLMs during text generation for more effective hallucination detection.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a variety of tasks in different domains. However, they sometimes generate responses that are logically coherent but factually incorrect or misleading, which is known as LLM hallucinations.
